firstMessage.content:
0.687 is an actual scored result, and the exact code is now public

I have just made 0.687|IT ACTUALLY WORKS public under Apache-2.0.

  • Official public score: 0.687, completed submission 58260754.
  • Exact scored source: Version 1, script version 368656391. Publishing changed the title and visibility, not the code.
  • This is an 18-class attribution task evaluated by balanced accuracy / macro recall.
  • All upstream credits are retained. The base is Areeb Ali's public v11 recipe; our addition is a small row-local, family-mass-preserving official-style residual after the native probabilities, plus preview/output guards. This is not a from-scratch ensemble.

Thanks to Areeb Ali and the upstream contributors for sharing the work this builds on. I am sharing the actual scored version so others can inspect it, reproduce it and suggest improvements.

A note on the timestamp: the Notebook still says it was updated two days ago because that is when Version 1 was saved/run. It was made public today. I have kept the scored source unchanged rather than creating a new run just to refresh the date.

What this result does and does not establish

Here, verified means Kaggle completed that submission with a public score of 0.687 and the published source matches its scored version. It is not a guarantee that every rerun will score identically.

I am not claiming the highest public score: Jose Padilla's public GLM-likelihood Notebook has a scored 0.689 Version 4. Notebook titles, latest versions and best scored versions can differ, so checking the actual version matters.

Our local residual experiment also failed its confidence/robustness admission checks. The original caveat remains visible in the Notebook. One public score does not establish a reliable causal gain over the earlier 0.684 base. The displayed short runtime is a public-sample preview, not the full hidden inference time.

Next target: 0.700. What would actually get us there?

I would like to turn this into an evidence-led community discussion:

  1. Validation that transfers. What prompt-disjoint split and response-per-prompt distribution best track the hidden task? How do you stress-test one, two or many responses per prompt without assuming a test-set grouping structure?
  2. Complementary errors. Which evidence adds genuinely different information to a strong public stack: token likelihood, embeddings or sparse style signals? Per-class recall and error overlap would be especially useful.
  3. OOF calibration and fusion. Has anyone obtained aligned, leakage-checked out-of-fold predictions for a full strong ensemble? I would prefer selecting temperatures/weights inside inner folds, then measuring them on held-out prompt groups.
  4. External-data hygiene. Which source, prompt-overlap and near-duplicate checks have helped avoid misleading local improvements?
  5. A practical compute budget. Which changes improve actual scored performance while keeping offline inference inside the competition's nine-hour limit? Runtime, failure cases and fallback behavior matter too.

The plan is to document each change, test it against a fixed comparator, and share the next verified improvement as public code if the evidence supports it. 0.700 is the target, not an achieved result or a promise.

If you try the Notebook, please share your scored version, validation protocol, runtime and what worked or failed. Suggestions, corrections and collaborative experiments are welcome.

Full code: https://www.kaggle.com/code/pengyipeng1/0-687-it-actually-works

Thanks for reading, and thanks again to everyone sharing reproducible work in this competition. Let's keep building and testing together.

3. **OOF calibration and fusion.** Has anyone obtained aligned, leakage-checked out-of-fold predictions for a full strong ensemble? I would prefer selecting temperatures/weights inside inner folds, then measuring them on held-out prompt groups.
4. **External-data hygiene.** Which source, prompt-overlap and near-duplicate checks have helped avoid misleading local improvements?
5. **A practical compute budget.** Which changes improve actual scored performance while keeping offline inference inside the competition's nine-hour limit? Runtime, failure cases and fallback behavior matter too.

The plan is to document each change, test it against a fixed comparator, and share the next verified improvement as public code if the evidence supports it. **0.700 is the target, not an achieved result or a promise.**

If you try the Notebook, please share your scored version, validation protocol, runtime and what worked or failed. Suggestions, corrections and collaborative experiments are welcome.

**Full code:** https://www.kaggle.com/code/pengyipeng1/0-687-it-actually-works

Thanks for reading, and thanks again to everyone sharing reproducible work in this competition. Let's keep building and testing together.
